title: INNER JOIN basics
explanation: Welcome to Level 4! Real databases split information into separate tables. The games table has a studio_id column, but not the studio's name. The name lives in the studios table. A JOIN glues two tables together side by side. ON says which columns should match: games.studio_id = studios.studio_id means 'line up each game with the studio that has the same ID'. Since both tables have a studio_id column, write table.column so SQL knows which one you mean. INNER JOIN only keeps rows that match in BOTH tables. Writing just JOIN means the same thing. Tip: give tables short nicknames with AS, like games AS g, to save typing.

example.code:
SELECT g.title, s.studio_name
FROM games AS g
INNER JOIN studios AS s
  ON g.studio_id = s.studio_id;

lines.explain: Show the title from games (g) and the studio name from studios (s).
Start with the games table, nicknamed g.
Glue on the studios table, nicknamed s.
Match each game to the studio with the same studio_id.

tasks.prompt: Show every game's title with the name of the studio that made it.
tasks.answer: SELECT games.title, studios.studio_name FROM games INNER JOIN studios ON games.studio_id = studios.studio_id;
hints: Join games to studios, matching on studio_id.
FROM games INNER JOIN studios ON games.studio_id = studios.studio_id

solution_lines.explain: Show the title from games and the studio name from studios.
Match rows where the studio IDs are the same.

tasks.prompt: Using nicknames g and s, show each game's title and the country its studio is from.
tasks.answer: SELECT g.title, s.country FROM games AS g INNER JOIN studios AS s ON g.studio_id = s.studio_id;
hints: Write games AS g and studios AS s, then use g. and s. in front of the columns.
SELECT g.title, s.country FROM games AS g INNER JOIN studios AS s ON g.studio_id = s.studio_id;

solution_lines.explain: Show the title from g (games) and the country from s (studios).

tasks.prompt: Show the title and studio name of every game made by a studio from Japan.
tasks.answer: SELECT g.title, s.studio_name FROM games AS g INNER JOIN studios AS s ON g.studio_id = s.studio_id WHERE s.country = 'Japan';
hints: Join first, then filter with WHERE. The country is in the studios table.

solution_lines.explain: Show the game title and studio name.
Only keep games whose studio is from Japan.

tasks.prompt: Show the title, studio name, and release year of every game made by a USA studio, sorted by title A to Z.
tasks.answer: SELECT g.title, s.studio_name, g.release_year FROM games AS g INNER JOIN studios AS s ON g.studio_id = s.studio_id WHERE s.country = 'USA' ORDER BY g.title ASC;
hints: Same as the last task, plus one more column and a sort.
... WHERE s.country = 'USA' ORDER BY g.title ASC

solution_lines.explain: Show the title, studio name, and release year.
Only keep games from USA studios.
Sort by title, A to Z.

tasks.prompt: Predict first: how many rows will this return? (There are 15 games and 12 studios.)
tasks.code:
SELECT s.studio_name
FROM games AS g
INNER JOIN studios AS s
  ON g.studio_id = s.studio_id;
hints: Every game has exactly one matching studio. Nintendo made 4 games, so how many times does Nintendo show up?
One row per matching game. Studios with no games, like Valve and Ubisoft, don't show up at all with INNER JOIN.

solution_lines.explain: Show the studio name for each matched row.
Glue on studios. Each game finds its one studio, so Nintendo appears 4 times.
Valve and Ubisoft have no matching games, so INNER JOIN leaves them out. That's 15 rows.

recap: You just learned INNER JOIN: glue two tables together with ON, use table.column to be clear, and remember that only rows matching in both tables are kept.
